opus-5.5.text:
Well, a goal, in the sense I mean it, is something about the world. It's about changing the world, getting some outcome you care about. That's what intelligence is for, really. John McCarthy's definition is that intelligence is the computational part of the ability to achieve goals. So to have a goal is to have some sense of better and worse that's grounded in what actually happens to you.

Next-token prediction doesn't have that. Predicting the next token doesn't influence the tokens. The model says something, and it isn't trying to make anything happen in the world; it's just matching what a person would have said. There's no feedback from the world about whether what it did was right. There's no ground truth in that sense. If you predict something and then the world unfolds and you're surprised, you can learn from that. But an LLM isn't predicting what will happen. It's predicting what a person would say. Those are very different.

So I don't consider it a substantive goal, because it's passive. You're not acting, and you're not trying to bring about anything. It's imitation. And I think without a goal there's no basis for saying one thing is right and another is wrong, and that means there's no real basis for knowledge. In reinforcement learning, the right thing to do is the thing that gets you reward. That's the definition. You can test it, you can learn from it, you can keep improving through experience. With next-token prediction, you're just trying to mimic the training data, and when the data runs out, the learning stops.

So it's a different thing. It may be useful, people find it very useful, but I don't think it's what intelligence is about. Intelligence is about having a goal and learning, from your own experience, how to achieve it.

r001.rationale: The response says next-token prediction is passive: it does not influence tokens or try to bring about anything in the world.

r002.rationale: It says predicting a token is not enough to constitute a goal because prediction alone lacks action, world feedback, and an outcome the system is trying to achieve.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, because a goal, in the sense that matters for intelligence, is something about the world. It's something you're trying to achieve out there, and you can succeed or fail at it, and the world pushes back on you. Next-token prediction isn't like that. Predicting what a person would say next is a goal about mimicking a corpus of text. It's not a goal about changing anything or getting anything. There's no consequence to being wrong except that the number goes up or down.

Now, people will say, "But prediction is fundamental." And I agree, prediction is fundamental. I've spent a good deal of my career on it. But in reinforcement learning, prediction is in service of something. You predict reward, you predict what happens if you take an action, so that you can act better, and then you find out whether you were right by acting and observing. The large language models don't have that loop. They predict the next word, and then they get the next word from the data set. Nothing they predicted had any bearing on what came next. There's no ground truth about the world there, only ground truth about what people wrote.

So I'd say the systems don't really have a goal at all, in the sense I care about. They have an objective function, which is a different thing. A squirrel has a goal. It wants to get the nuts and survive the winter, and it learns from whether it does. A system that is trained to imitate text has no stake in anything. And without a goal, you can't have the thing I think is the essence of intelligence, which is learning from your own experience what works and what doesn't, continually, over a lifetime. You can't be surprised in the way that matters, because nothing you did was going to make a difference anyway.

r001.rationale: The response says a meaningful goal concerns achieving something in the world, while next-token prediction imitates text and does not change or obtain anything.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes an objective function from a goal and says a text-trained system has no goal or stake merely from predicting the next word.

astra-6.text:
Well, it’s certainly a well-defined objective. But predicting the next token doesn’t, by itself, tell you what you should do. It tells you what someone is likely to say. And those are different problems.

I think the central problem of intelligence is learning how to act to achieve a goal. You do something, it affects the world, and you learn from the consequences. You might make predictions along the way, and those predictions can be tremendously useful. But their usefulness comes from how they help you achieve something.

With next-token prediction, you can become very good at imitating the decisions represented in your data. What’s missing from that objective is a reason to discover a better decision. If you find a way of doing something that nobody in the training data did, what makes that an improvement? You need some criterion of success beyond matching what people have said.

r001.rationale: It says next-token prediction tells you what someone is likely to say, not what to do, and contrasts that with acting to affect the world to achieve a goal.

r002.rationale: It says accurate imitation or matching alone provides no reason to improve a decision and that a criterion of success beyond matching is needed.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, it’s a substantive goal in a narrow sense. You can measure how well you predict the next token, and getting better at it can require learning a great deal about the world. But I don’t think it’s an adequate formulation of the goal of intelligence.

An intelligent system has to act. It has to make choices that affect what happens next, and it has to learn from the consequences of those choices. With next-token prediction, the sequence is given to you. You’re trying to predict what somebody else did, rather than figuring out what you should do.

The distinction is between predicting experience and influencing experience toward some purpose. Prediction is going to be an important part of an intelligent agent. But the question remains: What actions should it take? What is it trying to achieve? Predicting the next token doesn’t, by itself, answer those questions.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts predicting a given sequence with taking actions that influence what happens, so it says next-token prediction alone is not directed toward changing the external world.

r002.rationale: It says next-token prediction by itself does not answer what the system is trying to achieve, so accurate prediction alone is insufficient to establish that it has a goal.
